claim: Representational drift refers to the dynamic nature of neural representations in the brain despite the behavior being seemingly stable.
source: Representational drift refers to the dynamic nature of neural representations in the brain despite the behavior being seemingly stable.
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: Drift has been observed in many different brain regions.
source: Although drift has been observed in many different brain regions, the mechanisms underlying it are not known.
evidence: This statement is presented as established fact in the abstract, implicitly drawing on existing literature.

claim: The mechanisms underlying drift are not known.
source: Although drift has been observed in many different brain regions, the mechanisms underlying it are not known.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Intrinsic neural excitability is suggested to play a key role in regulating memory allocation.
source: Since intrinsic neural excitability is suggested to play a key role in regulating memory allocation, fluctuations of excitability could bias the reactivation of previously stored memory ensembles and therefore act as a motor for drift.
evidence: This is presented as an established suggestion in the literature.

claim: Fluctuations of excitability could bias the reactivation of previously stored memory ensembles and therefore act as a motor for drift.
source: Since intrinsic neural excitability is suggested to play a key role in regulating memory allocation, fluctuations of excitability could bias the reactivation of previously stored memory ensembles and therefore act as a motor for drift.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: A rate-based plastic recurrent neural network with slow fluctuations of intrinsic excitability can model drift.
source: Here, we propose a rate-based plastic recurrent neural network with slow fluctuations of intrinsic excitability.
evidence: This is the computational model proposed and implemented in the study.

claim: Subsequent reactivations of a neural ensemble can lead to drift of this ensemble.
source: We first show that subsequent reactivations of a neural ensemble can lead to drift of this ensemble.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the computational model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Drift is induced by co-activation of previously active neurons along with neurons with high excitability which leads to remodeling of the recurrent weights.
source: The model predicts that drift is induced by co-activation of previously active neurons along with neurons with high excitability which leads to remodeling of the recurrent weights.
evidence: This is a prediction from the computational model based on simulation results.

claim: The drifting ensemble is informative about its temporal history.
source: Consistent with previous experimental works, the drifting ensemble is informative about its temporal history.
evidence: This finding is supported by model simulations and is consistent with prior experimental work.

claim: The gradual nature of the drift is necessary for decoding temporal information from the activity of the ensemble.
source: Crucially, we show that the gradual nature of the drift is necessary for decoding temporal information from the activity of the ensemble.
evidence: This is a key finding from the computational model simulations.

claim: The memory is preserved and can be decoded by an output neuron having plastic synapses with the main region.
source: Finally, we show that the memory is preserved and can be decoded by an output neuron having plastic synapses with the main region.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations with a read-out neuron.

claim: Drift has been observed in sensory cortical areas.
source: Representational drift refers to the dynamic nature of internal representations as they have been observed in sensory cortical areas (Driscoll et al., 2017; Sadeh and Clopath, 2022; Driscoll et al., 2022) or the hippocampus (Ziv et al., 2013; Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018) despite stable behavior.
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Drift has been observed in the hippocampus.
source: Representational drift refers to the dynamic nature of internal representations as they have been observed in sensory cortical areas (Driscoll et al., 2017; Sadeh and Clopath, 2022; Driscoll et al., 2022) or the hippocampus (Ziv et al., 2013; Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018) despite stable behavior.
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Pyramidal neurons from the CA1 and CA3 regions form dynamic rather than static memory engrams.
source: It has even been suggested that pyramidal neurons from the CA1 and CA3 regions form dynamic rather than static memory engrams (Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018; Spalla et al., 2021), namely that the set of neurons encoding specific memories varies across days.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The set of neurons encoding specific memories varies across days.
source: It has even been suggested that pyramidal neurons from the CA1 and CA3 regions form dynamic rather than static memory engrams (Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018; Spalla et al., 2021), namely that the set of neurons encoding specific memories varies across days.
evidence: This is an explanation of what dynamic memory engrams means, supported by citations.

claim: Retraining of a fear memory task induces a turnover of the memory engram in the amygdala.
source: In the amygdala, retraining of a fear memory task induces a turnover of the memory engram (Cho et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: Plasticity mechanisms have been proposed to compensate for drift and to provide a stable read-out of the neural code.
source: Additionally, plasticity mechanisms have been proposed to compensate for drift and to provide a stable read-out of the neural code (Rule and O'Leary, 2022), suggesting that information is maintained.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior computational work.

claim: Information is maintained despite drift.
source: Additionally, plasticity mechanisms have been proposed to compensate for drift and to provide a stable read-out of the neural code (Rule and O'Leary, 2022), suggesting that information is maintained.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that plasticity mechanisms can provide stable read-out.

claim: Drift might be a general mechanism with dynamical representations observed in various brain regions.
source: Altogether, this line of evidence suggests that drift might be a general mechanism with dynamical representations observed in various brain regions.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the cited evidence.

claim: Drift is often thought to arise from variability of internal states.
source: Drift is often thought to arise from variability of internal states (Sadeh and Clopath, 2022), neurogenesis (Rechavi et al., 2022; Driscoll et al., 2017) or synaptic turnover (Attardo et al., 2015) combined with noise (Kossio et al., 2021; Manz and Memmesheimer, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior theoretical and experimental work.

claim: Drift is often thought to arise from neurogenesis.
source: Drift is often thought to arise from variability of internal states (Sadeh and Clopath, 2022), neurogenesis (Rechavi et al., 2022; Driscoll et al., 2017) or synaptic turnover (Attardo et al., 2015) combined with noise (Kossio et al., 2021; Manz and Memmesheimer, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Drift is often thought to arise from synaptic turnover combined with noise.
source: Drift is often thought to arise from variability of internal states (Sadeh and Clopath, 2022), neurogenesis (Rechavi et al., 2022; Driscoll et al., 2017) or synaptic turnover (Attardo et al., 2015) combined with noise (Kossio et al., 2021; Manz and Memmesheimer, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Neurons having high excitability are preferentially allocated to memory ensembles.
source: On the other hand, excitability might also play a role in memory allocation (Zhou et al., 2009; Mau et al., 2020; Rogerson et al., 2014; Silva et al., 2009), so that neurons having high excitability are preferentially allocated to memory ensembles (Cai et al., 2016; Rashid et al., 2016; Silva et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Excitability is known to fluctuate over timescales from hours to days in the amygdala.
source: Moreover, excitability is known to fluctuate over timescales from hours to days, in the amygdala (Rashid et al., 2016), the hippocampus (Cai et al., 2016; Grosmark and Buzsáki, 2016), or the cortex (Huber et al., 2013; Levenstein et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Excitability is known to fluctuate over timescales from hours to days in the hippocampus.
source: Moreover, excitability is known to fluctuate over timescales from hours to days, in the amygdala (Rashid et al., 2016), the hippocampus (Cai et al., 2016; Grosmark and Buzsáki, 2016), or the cortex (Huber et al., 2013; Levenstein et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Excitability is known to fluctuate over timescales from hours to days in the cortex.
source: Moreover, excitability is known to fluctuate over timescales from hours to days, in the amygdala (Rashid et al., 2016), the hippocampus (Cai et al., 2016; Grosmark and Buzsáki, 2016), or the cortex (Huber et al., 2013; Levenstein et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Subsequent reactivations of a neural ensemble at different time points could be biased by excitability.
source: Subsequent reactivations of a neural ensemble at different time points could therefore be biased by excitability (Mau et al., 2022), which varies at similar timescales than drift (Mau et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Excitability varies at similar timescales as drift.
source: Subsequent reactivations of a neural ensemble at different time points could therefore be biased by excitability (Mau et al., 2022), which varies at similar timescales than drift (Mau et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Fluctuations of excitability could act as a cellular mechanism for drift.
source: Altogether, this evidence suggest that fluctuations of excitability could act as a cellular mechanism for drift (Mau et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by a citation.

claim: Slow fluctuations of excitability can induce neural ensembles to drift in the network.
source: As a proof of principle, we first show that slow fluctuations of excitability can induce neural ensembles to drift in the network.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the computational model.

claim: Neural activity of the drifting ensemble is informative about the temporal structure of the memory.
source: Consistent with previous works (Rubin et al., 2015; Clopath et al., 2017; Mau et al., 2018; Miller et al., 2018), we show that neural activity of the drifting ensemble is informative about the temporal structure of the memory.
evidence: This is a finding from the model that is consistent with prior work.

claim: Fluctuations of excitability can be useful for time-stamping memories.
source: This suggest that fluctuations of excitability can be useful for time-stamping memories (i.e. for making the neural ensemble informative about the time at which it was form).
evidence: This is an inference from the model results.

claim: The content of the memory itself can be steadily maintained using a read-out neuron and local plasticity rule.
source: Finally, we confirmed that the content of the memory itself can be steadily maintained using a read-out neuron and local plasticity rule, consistently with previous computational works (Rule and O'Leary, 2022).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the model and is consistent with prior computational work.

claim: Memories are encoded in sparse neural ensembles that are activated during learning.
source: Many studies have shown that memories are encoded in sparse neural ensembles that are activated during learning and many of the same cells are reactivated during recall, underlying a stable neural representation (Josselyn and Tonegawa, 2020; Poo et al., 2016; Mau et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Many of the same cells are reactivated during recall, underlying a stable neural representation.
source: Many studies have shown that memories are encoded in sparse neural ensembles that are activated during learning and many of the same cells are reactivated during recall, underlying a stable neural representation (Josselyn and Tonegawa, 2020; Poo et al., 2016; Mau et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Subsequent reactivations of the ensemble can happen spontaneously during replay, retraining or during a memory recall task.
source: After learning, subsequent reactivations of the ensemble can happen spontaneously during replay, retraining or during a memory recall task (e.g. following presentation of a cue Josselyn and Tonegawa, 2020; Káli and Dayan, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: During the first stimulation, a neural ensemble is formed composed of neurons that have high excitability at the time of stimulation.
source: While stimulating the naive network on the first day, we observed the formation of a neural ensemble: some neurons gradually increase their firing rate (Figure 1b and c, neurons 10–20, time steps 1000–3000) during the stimulation. We observed that these neurons are highly recurrently connected (Figure 1d, leftmost matrix) suggesting that they form an assembly. This assembly is composed of neurons that have a high excitability (Figure 1a, neurons 10–20 have increase excitability) at the time of the stimulation.
evidence: This is observed in the model simulations and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Neurons forming an assembly are highly recurrently connected.
source: We observed that these neurons are highly recurrently connected (Figure 1d, leftmost matrix) suggesting that they form an assembly.
evidence: This is observed in the model simulations and shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Further stimulations of the network induce a remodeling of the synaptic weights.
source: We then show that further stimulations of the network induce a remodeling of the synaptic weights.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the model simulations.

claim: During the second stimulation, neurons from the previous assembly are reactivated along with neurons having high excitability at the time of the second stimulation.
source: During the second stimulation for instance (Figure 1b and c, time steps 4000–6000), neurons from the previous assembly (10–20) are reactivated along with neurons having high excitability at the time of the second stimulation (Figure 1a, neurons 20–30).
evidence: This is observed in the model simulations and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Across several days, recurrent weights from previous assemblies tend to decrease while others increase.
source: Moreover, across several days, recurrent weights from previous assemblies tend to decrease while others increase (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is observed in the model simulations and shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Neurons from the original assembly tend to be replaced by other neurons, either from the latest assembly or from the pool of neurons having high excitability.
source: Indeed, neurons from the original assembly (Figure 1c, red traces) tend to be replaced by other neurons, either from the latest assembly or from the pool of neurons having high excitability.
evidence: This is observed in the model simulations and shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Each new stimulation updates the ensemble according to the current distribution of excitability, inducing a drift towards neurons with high excitability.
source: Overall, each new stimulation updates the ensemble according to the current distribution of excitability, inducing a drift towards neurons with high excitability.
evidence: This is a summary of the model behavior observed in simulations.

claim: The drift rate does not depend on the size of the original ensemble.
source: Finally, in our model, the drift rate does not depend on the size of the original ensemble (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Methods).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the model simulations and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The correlation between patterns of activity after just after encoding decreases across days.
source: We first observed that the correlation between patterns of activity after just after encoding decreases across days (Figure 2a, Methods), indicating that after each day, the newly formed ensemble resembles less the original one.
evidence: This is observed in the model simulations and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: After each day, the newly formed ensemble resembles less the original one.
source: We first observed that the correlation between patterns of activity after just after encoding decreases across days (Figure 2a, Methods), indicating that after each day, the newly formed ensemble resembles less the original one.
evidence: This is inferred from the decreasing correlation observed in simulations.

claim: The patterns of activity differ across days and should be informative about the absolute day from which they were recorded.
source: Because the patterns of activity differ across days, they should be informative about the absolute day from which they were recorded.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the observation that patterns differ across days.

claim: The day decoder perfectly outputs the reactivation day as compared to using shuffled data.
source: We found that the day decoder perfectly outputs the reactivation day as compared to using shuffled data (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the model simulations and shown in Figure 2c.

claim: When E=0, the patterns of activity are not informative about the order of reactivations.
source: In this case, the patterns of activity are not informative about the order of reactivations.
evidence: This is inferred from the model behavior when there is no drift.

claim: When E=3, the patterns of activity are not informative about the order of the reactivations.
source: In this regime, the patterns of activity are not informative about the order of the reactivations either.
evidence: This is inferred from the model behavior when drift is complete.

claim: The results are independent of the specific architecture of the model.
source: Finally, we sought to test whether the results are independent on the specific architecture of the model.
evidence: This is tested through additional simulations with different model architectures.

claim: Similar drifting behavior is observed when excitability is defined as a change in the slope of the activation function rather than of the threshold.
source: To that end, we defined a change of excitability as a change in the slope of the activation function, rather than of the threshold (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Methods). We also used sparse recurrent synaptic weights instead of the original all-to-all connectivity matrix (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Methods). In both cases, we observed a similar drifting behavior and were able to decode the temporal order in which the memory evolved.
evidence: This is demonstrated in additional model simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Similar drifting behavior is observed when using sparse recurrent synaptic weights instead of all-to-all connectivity.
source: To that end, we defined a change of excitability as a change in the slope of the activation function, rather than of the threshold (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Methods). We also used sparse recurrent synaptic weights instead of the original all-to-all connectivity matrix (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Methods). In both cases, we observed a similar drifting behavior and were able to decode the temporal order in which the memory evolved.
evidence: This is demonstrated in additional model simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The output neuron can steadily decode the memory.
source: We found that the output neuron could steadily decode the memory (i.e. it has a higher firing than in the case where the output weights are randomly shuffled; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the model simulations and shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The output neuron's ability to decode memory is due to the fact that weights are plastic under Hebbian learning.
source: This is due to the fact that weights are plastic under Hebbian learning, as shown by Rule and O'Leary, 2022.
evidence: This is an inference from the model mechanism, consistent with prior work.

claim: The output weights change across time, with weights from neurons that no longer belong to the ensemble decreasing and weights from newly recruited neurons increasing.
source: We confirmed that this was induced by a change in the output weights across time (Figure 3c). In particular, the weights from neurons that no longer belong to the ensemble are decreased while weights from newly recruited neurons are increased, so that the center of mass of the weights distribution drifts across time (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is observed in the model simulations and shown in Figures 3c and 3d.

claim: The center of mass of the weights distribution drifts across time.
source: In particular, the weights from neurons that no longer belong to the ensemble are decreased while weights from newly recruited neurons are increased, so that the center of mass of the weights distribution drifts across time (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is observed in the model simulations and shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The quality of the read-out decreases with the rate of the drift.
source: Finally, we found that the quality of the read-out decreases with the rate of the drift (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Methods).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the model simulations and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The network is able to encode two different memories and excitability can make two ensembles drift.
source: Finally, we tested whether the network is able to encode two different memories and whether excitability could make two ensembles drift.
evidence: This is tested in additional model simulations.

claim: When two ensembles are formed, both show similar drift as when only one ensemble was formed.
source: We found that, day after day, the two ensembles show a similar drift than when only one ensemble was formed (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the model simulations and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: For both contexts, the temporal order of the reactivations can be decoded for a certain range of excitability amplitude.
source: For both contexts, the temporal order of the reactivations can be decoded for a certain range of excitability amplitude (Figure 2—figure supplement 4b).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the model simulations and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4b.

claim: Using two output decoders allows decoding both memories independently.
source: Finally, we found that using two output decoders allowed us to decode both memories independently.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the model simulations.

claim: The output weights associated to both ensembles are remodeled to follow the drifting ensembles, but are not affected by the reactivation of the other ensemble.
source: The output weights associated to both ensembles are remodeled to follow the drifting ensembles, but are not affected by the reactivation of the other ensemble (Figure 2—figure supplement 4c).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the model simulations and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4c.

claim: Both output neurons are able to 'track' the reactivation of their associated ensemble while not responding to the other ensemble.
source: Indeed, both neurons are able to 'track' the reactivation of their associated ensemble while not responding to the other ensemble (Figure 2—figure supplement 4d).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the model simulations and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4d.

claim: The model suggests a potential cellular mechanism for the emergence of drift that can serve a computational purpose by 'time-stamping' memories while still being able to decode the memory across time.
source: Overall, our model suggests a potential cellular mechanisms for the emergence of drift that can serve a computational purpose by 'time-stamping' memories while still being able to decode the memory across time.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the model results.

claim: The ability for the neural ensemble to encode the order of past reactivations requires drift to be gradual.
source: However, the ability for the neural ensemble to encode the order of past reactivations requires drift to be gradual (i.e. requires consecutive patterns of activity to remain correlated across days).
evidence: This is inferred from the model results showing that intermediate excitability levels are necessary for temporal decoding.

claim: The result that gradual drift enables temporal decoding is consistent with previous works showing gradual change in neural representations.
source: This result is consistent with the previous works showing gradual change in neural representations, that allows for decoding temporal information of the ensemble (Rubin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as consistency with prior work.

claim: Gradual drifts could support complex cognitive mechanisms like mental time-travel during memory recall.
source: Moreover, such gradual drifts could support complex cognitive mechanisms like mental time-travel during memory recall (Rubin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by a citation.

claim: In the model, drift is induced by co-activation of the previously formed ensemble and neurons with high excitability at the time of the reactivation.
source: In our model, drift is induced by co-activation of the previously formed ensemble and neurons with high excitability at the time of the reactivation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic description of how drift occurs in the model.

claim: The pool of neurons having high excitability can 'time-stamps' memory ensembles by biasing allocation of these ensembles.
source: The pool of neurons having high excitability can therefore 'time-stamps' memory ensembles by biasing allocation of these ensembles (Clopath et al., 2017; Mau et al., 2018; Rubin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference from the model mechanism, consistent with prior work.

claim: Time-stamping mechanism could help link memories that are temporally close and dissociate those which are spaced by longer time.
source: We suggest that such time-stamping mechanism could also help link memories that are temporally close and dissociate those which are spaced by longer time (Driscoll et al., 2022; Mau et al., 2020; Aimone et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion supported by citations.

claim: The pool of neurons with high excitability varies across time so that any new memory ensemble is allocated to neurons which are shared with other ensembles formed around the same time.
source: Indeed, the pool of neurons with high excitability varies across time so that any new memory ensemble is allocated to neurons which are shared with other ensembles formed around the same time.
evidence: This is an inference from the model mechanism.

claim: This mechanism could be complementary to the learning-induced increase in excitability observed in amygdala, hippocampal CA1 and dentate gyrus.
source: This mechanism could be complementary to the learning-induced increase in excitability observed in amygdala (Rashid et al., 2016), hippocampal CA1 (Cai et al., 2016) and dentate gyrus (Pignatelli et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: The study intended to model drift in the firing rates, as opposed to a drift in the turning curve, of the neurons.
source: Finally, we intended to model drift in the firing rates, as opposed to a drift in the turning curve, of the neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about the modeling approach.

claim: Recent studies suggest that drifts in the mean firing rate and tuning curve arise from two different mechanisms.
source: Recent studies suggest that drifts in the mean firing rate and tuning curve arise from two different mechanisms (Geva et al., 2023; Khatib et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Experience drives a drift in neurons turning curve while the passage of time drives a drift in neurons firing rate.
source: Experience drives a drift in neurons turning curve while the passage of time drives a drift in neurons firing rate.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from recent studies.

claim: The study is consistent with findings that the passage of time drives a drift in neurons firing rate by providing a possible mechanism for this drift driven by dynamical excitability.
source: In this sense, our study is consistent with these findings by providing a possible mechanism for a drift in the mean firing rates of the neurons driven a dynamical excitability.
evidence: This is stated as consistency with prior findings.

claim: Drift can depend on any experience having an impact on excitability dynamics such as exercise.
source: Our work suggests that drift can depend on any experience having an impact on excitability dynamics such as exercise as previously shown experimentally (Rechavi et al., 2022; de Snoo et al., 2023) but also neurogenesis (Aimone et al., 2006; Tran et al., 2022; Rechavi et al., 2022), sleep (Levenstein et al., 2017) or increase in dopamine level (Chowdhury et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: Drift can depend on neurogenesis.
source: Our work suggests that drift can depend on any experience having an impact on excitability dynamics such as exercise as previously shown experimentally (Rechavi et al., 2022; de Snoo et al., 2023) but also neurogenesis (Aimone et al., 2006; Tran et al., 2022; Rechavi et al., 2022), sleep (Levenstein et al., 2017) or increase in dopamine level (Chowdhury et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: Drift can depend on sleep.
source: Our work suggests that drift can depend on any experience having an impact on excitability dynamics such as exercise as previously shown experimentally (Rechavi et al., 2022; de Snoo et al., 2023) but also neurogenesis (Aimone et al., 2006; Tran et al., 2022; Rechavi et al., 2022), sleep (Levenstein et al., 2017) or increase in dopamine level (Chowdhury et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: Drift can depend on increase in dopamine level.
source: Our work suggests that drift can depend on any experience having an impact on excitability dynamics such as exercise as previously shown experimentally (Rechavi et al., 2022; de Snoo et al., 2023) but also neurogenesis (Aimone et al., 2006; Tran et al., 2022; Rechavi et al., 2022), sleep (Levenstein et al., 2017) or increase in dopamine level (Chowdhury et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: The work is a proof of principle which highlights the importance of considering excitability when studying drift.
source: Overall, our work is a proof of principle which highlights the importance of considering excitability when studying drift, although further work would be needed to test this link experimentally.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the nature and implications of the work.

claim: Further work would be needed to test the link between excitability and drift experimentally.
source: Overall, our work is a proof of principle which highlights the importance of considering excitability when studying drift, although further work would be needed to test this link experimentally.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the computational study.
